intro: Today's AI news carries a unmistakable theme: pushback. From thousands of Australian artists — including Indigenous creators calling AI-generated art "Temu slop" — rallying against proposed copyright changes, to Apple's new CEO insisting the company won't "ship AI for AI's sake," to a federal judge greenlighting an NAACP pollution lawsuit against xAI's data center, the humans are pushing back on all fronts. We've also got a Senate bill proposing two years of income support for AI-displaced workers, a Goldman Sachs finding that those workers are struggling to land new jobs, and — on the lighter side — a journalist who beat Meta to market by building a $50 DIY AI Tamagotchi with a dev kit and some vibe coding.

stories.title: Australian artists rally against proposed AI copyright changes allowing scraping
stories.summary: Pitjantjatjara artist Sally Scales, who chairs the National Gallery of Australia's First Nations advisory group, has spoken out against AI systems that scrape and replicate Indigenous Australian art, calling the output 'Temu slop.' Meanwhile, over 3,000 creative professionals in Prime Minister Albanese's own electorate of Grayndler are organizing against the federal government's proposal to allow AI companies to scrape online content, creating political discomfort in his own backyard.
stories.opinion: The backlash is broadening from constitutional lawyers to the artists themselves, and the fact that it's reaching Albanese's own electorate adds real political pressure that could force revisions to the proposal.

sources.title: Disquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposal
AI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist says

cluster.reason: Both cover Australian artists' backlash against the federal government's proposed AI copyright changes that would allow scraping of their work.

stories.title: Patagonia's people-first leadership philosophy and AI workforce impact roundup
stories.summary: Patagonia Chief People and Culture Officer Theresita Richard shared the company's philosophy of treating employees 'like humans' and 'like adults' at the Charter Workplace Summit, emphasizing authenticity, entrepreneurship, agency, and mutual accountability. The article also covers AI-and-work developments: a US Senate bill proposing two years of income support for AI-displaced workers, an Apollo Global Management report finding 'zero financial payoff' from AI outside tech, Goldman Sachs data showing AI-displaced workers take longer to find new jobs, and Anthropic's IPO filing identifying loss of worker trust as a risk factor.
stories.opinion: The juxtaposition of Patagonia's human-centered culture with data showing AI's uneven economic payoff and growing displacement concerns underscores a widening gap between companies treating the AI transition thoughtfully and those that aren't.

stories.title: Apple CEO Ternus says the company doesn't 'want to ship AI for AI's sake'
stories.summary: Apple CEO John Ternus, who took the role in September 2026, defended Apple's AI positioning in a Wired interview. He acknowledged criticism over being behind on AI, particularly after delaying a more powerful Siri that launched in summer 2026, but said he likes where Apple is and emphasized that users shouldn't have to think about whether AI or traditional software powers a feature. When asked about AI agents making apps unnecessary, Ternus called product creation 'a deeply human and personal thing.'
stories.opinion: The messaging is classic Apple restraint, but after years of playing catch-up on AI, the 'we don't ship for AI's sake' line will only hold if Apple Intelligence delivers meaningfully differentiated user experiences soon.

stories.title: Verge writer builds $50 DIY AI Tamagotchi before Meta's Muse Charm ships
stories.summary: Sean Hollister of The Verge built a DIY AI Tamagotchi pendant for $50 using a Waveshare ESP32-S3 touchscreen devkit, connecting it to Meta's Muse AI cloud with open-source code. The device features push-to-talk AI interaction, cute avatars, and doubles as a pocket watch and remote camera viewfinder. While it lacks the Muse Charm's cameras and 5G radio, Hollister found the build required significant 'vibe coding' to add features like smart home control.
stories.opinion: A fun demonstration of how accessible AI hardware tinkering has become, though it also highlights that Meta's upcoming Muse Charm will need to offer substantially more polish to justify a premium over hobbyist alternatives.

stories.title: TechCrunch promotes Founder Summit in Boston on November 4
stories.summary: TechCrunch is promoting its Founder Summit happening November 4, 2026 at Boston's SoWa Power Station, featuring a Networking Lounge powered by Braindate, roundtables, breakout sessions, an Expo Hall, and a closing reception. The event is presented by Fidelity Private Shares and targets founders and VCs.
stories.opinion: Event promotion rather than news; only notable as a signal of continued strong demand for in-person founder and VC networking events.

stories.title: High-street brands stage comeback with AI stylists and A-list collaborations
stories.summary: High street brands like Gap, M&S, and Topshop are borrowing strategies from luxury fashion, pursuing A-list celebrity collaborations, AI-powered styling services, and enhanced shopping experiences to win over sustainability-conscious consumers who had drifted toward luxury labels or ultra-cheap online retailers.
stories.opinion: AI styling tools are an interesting differentiator for mid-market fashion, but the real test is whether these brands can sustain the strategy beyond the novelty phase and translate it into lasting customer loyalty.

stories.title: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI Colossus data center pollution to proceed
stories.summary: A federal judge denied xAI's motion to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit alleging the company operated gas turbines at its Colossus data center near Memphis without required Clean Air Act permits. Judge Debra M. Brown rejected xAI's arguments that the turbines qualify as exempt mobile sources. The NAACP claims xAI installed at least 35 combustion turbines without preconstruction or operating air permits. The ruling comes amid growing backlash against data centers, including a New York moratorium on new facilities.
stories.opinion: A significant legal precedent that could force AI infrastructure companies to comply with existing environmental regulations rather than claiming exemptions, and adds to mounting political pressure on data center expansion.

tweet_headlines.source_text:
I open-sourced 43 agent skills for shipping real products. No coding.

Everything I learned from 190K installs and sign ups.

Why was it needed?

Popular AI engineering skill collections are for people who work with the code a lot. They skip discovery, go-to-market, and product analytics. 

I wanted to create something for people focused on the user and business value. A set of skills that helps you: 

→ research the market and competitors
→ listen to the users, e.g., on Reddit
→ identify your value proposition and value curve
→ decide how to grow
→ learn from people using your product for real

Then agents build, review each other's work, and ship. You approve the release.

Inside, 6 packs from the first idea to paying users:

→ Product (8): discovering what to build
→ AI shipping (10): a reliable, secure AI-built app you can sign off on
→ App stack (14): sign-in, payments, email, analytics, and legal pages
→ Agent teams (4): other agents as partners, e.g., Codex
→ Agent harness (6): a reliable setup, with you in the loop
→ Work humanizer (1): work writing that doesn't read as AI

You don't have to memorize them. Type /start-here and it explains where you are, what's done, and the next steps.

Free repo (GitHub): https://t.co/VSLGyLdMsn

If it helps, star the repo so the next person finds it.

tweet_headlines.author: pratikg
tweet_headlines.headline: Microsoft's Mage, a __4B open-weight computer-use agent__, scores 66% on OSWorld-Verified — just below the human benchmark — and runs 19 moves a minute on a Mac mini.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
🚨 RESULTS: @Microsoft's Mage, the 4B open-weight computer-use agent, on my 64GB M5 Pro Mac mini, as promised.

Microsoft quietly released it this morning.

Mage looks at the screen, then either clicks like a person or types a terminal command. It decides at every step.

The model card made a big claim. 66% on OSWorld-Verified, a few points under the 72.4% humans score. Qwen3.6-27B, almost 6x its size, scores 63.9%.

I wanted to see it on my own machine. There was no MLX build yet, so I converted it myself. (Link below) 

At 4-bit it fits in under 9GB of memory. It runs 96 tok/s at 512 context and 34 tok/s at the full 32K.

Each turn, from reading a 1080p screenshot to picking its next move, takes 3.1 seconds. That's up to 19 moves a minute, on a Mac mini.

I gave it 3 real tasks. It totaled a CSV's revenue correctly and renamed a file on the first try. It missed the Dark Mode toggle by 42 pixels at 4-bit. Full precision nailed it.

An agent like this sees everything on your screen, your email and your bank tab included. I'd rather those screenshots never leave my desk. With Mage, they don't.

It's Apache 2.0, so anyone can build on it.

tweet_headlines.author: 0xChaseTM
tweet_headlines.headline: SpaceX AI engineer Lauren Tan demos how __pstack routes tasks through playbooks__, builds verification skills per repo, and blocks merges without reproducible evidence.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
this is f***ing gold

SpaceXAI engineer Lauren Tan shows how pstack works:

start with /poteto-mode to route the task through the right playbook

> Define the task

goal / constraints / observable_success

/poteto-mode selects the playbook. skills such as /how, /why and /architect supply context and design work when needed

> Verify the running app

/create-verification-skill

Builds and trials a repo-specific procedure:

launch → doctor → drive → evidence → cleanup

The proof depends on the change:

→ UI: complete the affected user journey
→ CLI: capture the command, output and exit status
→ storage: read back the written value
→ performance: compare profiles under equivalent conditions

> Hand off the tested change

tested_commit / diff / commands + results / evidence_paths

Failed checks send the change back for repair

Unavailable checks stay listed under unverified_checks, with the missing dependency explained

> Prevent recurring failures

/reflect - captures the lesson

/correct - helps encode it through architecture, types, lint, CI or tests

predictable mechanical work moves into scripts so the next run can reuse it

Save this to spend less time supervising fixes ↓

tweet_headlines.author: vasuman
tweet_headlines.headline: Varick says the __market for AI transformation__ will grow 100x in three years — and finance is the best beachhead.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
We're still in the early innings of AI transformation. Varick estimates the market for AI transformation will grow 100x over the next 3 years.

Finance is one of the best places to start, for a few reasons:

- Most of the time is spent waiting. One invoice exception takes 25 minutes of work, but 11 days to clear.
- Finance leaves a better data trail than any other function. Every invoice, approval, and journal entry is timestamped somewhere, even if half of it lives in Excel.
- Much of the work is rule-based. You can't afford for agents to hallucinate in the finance function, and by incorporating heavy determinism, you de-risk the agents.

In the article below, our COO Eyad breaks down the exact playbook we've used to roll out AI in finance at some of the largest companies in the world.

If you're working on agents in finance, or you're an FDE, this playbook is a gold mine.

tweet_headlines.author: AISystems_hq
tweet_headlines.headline: Claude's desktop app Code tab lets non-coders __build client portals and calculators in plain English__ — describe the end goal, have it interview you, then let it build.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
You won't write a line of code. It builds client portals, calculators, and small tools, you describe them, you never read code.

It's not for you if you want a one-off doc or spreadsheet (that's Cowork), a single image (that's ChatGPT), a chart you'll look at once (that's an Artifact), or just an answer to a question (that's Claude Chat). Still here? Then it's for you.

Setup takes a few minutes: download the Claude desktop app, Pro is enough, open the Code tab, make one empty folder with nothing private in it, and point Claude at that folder.

The prompt that works: tell Claude it's the developer and you're the owner, you don't read code, plain English only. Give it your end goal, have it interview you one question at a time, make it show you the plan, then let it build.

The constant loop: run it and click through it like a customer would, write down what's wrong as a numbered list in plain words, paste the list back, and repeat until the list is empty. Read every permission it asks for before you click allow.

What to build: a client portal where people see where their project stands, a quote calculator for your website, a tool that turns your messy export into the monthly report you send. Build the thing you keep doing by hand in a spreadsheet.

Don't look like every AI tool: screenshot one app whose look you like, drop it in the folder, and tell Claude to match it for all the styling. Stop typing "make it look good."

What it costs: Pro is enough to start. Start a new chat for every task, point it at the files in the folder instead of pasting big text, and type /usage to see where you stand. You pay for every wrong turn, so ask for the plan first.

Delete the belief that the Code tab is for developers, the one giant chat you never close, the weekend build nobody ever opens, and the idea you'll start once things calm down.

Follow @AISystems_hq for more Claude setups.
